idiom_name: one access object per table + one record structure per row + client-owned connection
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: create one object (or module) per table or updatable view; give it one method per statement and let each method own exactly one parameterized SQL string - no other code may contain SQL for that table. Rows cross the boundary as records: return tuples, structs, hashes or framework rowsets, never domain objects, and accept the same shape on insert/update. The gateway borrows the connection, pool or session from its caller and never opens, closes or commits one itself, so transactions and units of work can span several gateways. Keep cross-table reporting out of the write path: put it in a query object or finder that also returns records. Where the platform provides a per-table accessor or a rowset abstraction (DataAdapter/DataTable, datasets, TableQuery, table builders), use it instead of hand-rolling the shell.
code_sketch:
gateway = UsersGateway(connection)          # one per table, connection borrowed
# methods own exactly one statement each:
row   = gateway.find_by_id(id)              # -> Record (tuple/struct/hash)
new_id = gateway.insert(record)             # parameters bound, never interpolated
count = gateway.update_name(id, name)
gateway.delete(id)
# caller owns the transaction:
with transaction(connection):
    orders.insert(order); lines.insert_all(lines)
pitfalls: Letting a second code path keep its own SQL for the same table - the gateway is then a convention, not a boundary.
Opening or committing the connection inside the gateway; the caller can no longer make several gateway calls atomic.
Interpolating values into SQL text instead of binding parameters, which reintroduces injection at the one place that was supposed to be safe.
Growing the object into a per-schema god gateway with cross-table joins and business rules instead of splitting it or adding a query object.

Wrong move: gateway methods returning the application's domain or framework entity type instead of a record -> the gateway must know entity constructors, relations and change tracking, so every schema tweak ripples into the domain instead of stopping at the gateway -> return a plain row record and map it to a domain object at the boundary if one is wanted.

Wrong move: assembling statements inside the gateway from shared SQL fragment builders and caller flags -> there is no longer a single complete statement to grep, review or hand to a DBA, and dialect knowledge leaks back out to callers -> keep one full parameterized statement literal per method and move genuinely dynamic queries into a dedicated query object.

Wrong move: finders that return a zero-value record or silently null when the SELECT matched nothing -> callers cannot tell absent from default-valued rows and a read of a deleted row becomes an overwriting write -> make absence explicit in the signature (Option/Optional/nil or an empty record set) so every caller must handle the missing row.
